lesson.title: Object Permanence: Why 'Out of Sight' Isn't Always 'Out of Mind'
lesson.summary: Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they can't be seen, heard, or touched, is a hallmark achievement of the sensorimotor stage, though research since Piaget suggests infants may grasp at least parts of it earlier than he believed.
lesson.body:
Object permanence is the understanding that an object keeps existing even when it is out of view. It sounds almost too obvious to be interesting to adults, but for very young infants it is a genuine cognitive achievement, and it is the reason games like peekaboo are so captivating: for an infant who has not yet developed this understanding, a hidden face may seem to have actually disappeared.

Piaget tested this with a simple, now classic procedure: he hid an interesting object under a cloth in full view of an infant. Younger infants, roughly under eight months by Piaget's account, typically did not search for the object at all, behaving as if it had simply ceased to exist once it was out of sight. Older infants began reaching for and uncovering the hidden object, which Piaget took as evidence that they now understood it still existed.

A particularly famous finding from this research is the A-not-B error. An infant who has just succeeded several times in finding a toy hidden at one location, location A, will often keep searching at location A even after watching an experimenter clearly hide the same toy at a new location, location B. Piaget interpreted this as a sign that the object concept was still incomplete, typically observing it somewhere around eight to twelve months of age. Piaget proposed that a fuller, more flexible grasp of object permanence was generally in place by around eighteen to twenty-four months, which lines up with the transition toward the mental representation that defines the next stage, the preoperational stage.

Later research has meaningfully complicated this picture, in a way that is worth understanding rather than glossing over. The developmental psychologist Renee Baillargeon and other researchers used a different kind of method, called violation-of-expectation, that measures how long infants look at an event rather than requiring them to physically search for a hidden object. Because infants tend to look longer at events that seem physically impossible, researchers can infer what an infant expects without needing the infant to plan and execute a reach. Using this approach, studies found that infants as young as a few months old sometimes look longer at impossible outcomes involving a hidden object, suggesting they may have some implicit understanding that the object still exists well before they show it through active searching.

The most reasonable way to read this body of research is as a competence versus performance question rather than a simple case of Piaget being wrong: young infants may understand more than Piaget's original task could reveal, because succeeding at his hiding task requires not just the underlying concept but also enough motor planning and memory to actually reach for and uncover the object, abilities that themselves take time to develop.
